stops.name: Prague, David Oppenheimer and the great library
stops.campa: In Prague sits Samuel's nephew, David Oppenheimer, chief rabbi and the age's greatest collector of Hebrew books. Prince Eugene of Savoy carries back from the Turkish wars a trove of manuscripts and lays them, through the Oberfaktor's hand, into that library: thousands of volumes that will one day cross to Oxford and rest in the Bodleian. The uncle's war-gold and the nephew's scholarship are one enterprise: the Court Jew builds not only armies' bread but the memory of a people in ink.

stops.name: Heidelberg, the birth of Joseph Süss, the mirror to come
stops.campa: Back in Heidelberg, where Samuel's own career began, a boy is born into the wider Oppenheimer kin to a Jewish tax-collector and his wife: Joseph Süss Oppenheimer, 'Jud Süss.' He will become court Jew to the Duke of Württemberg and climb as high as Samuel and higher, and then fall as Samuel never quite did: seized on his patron's death, tried, and hanged in an iron cage over Stuttgart in 1738. The same arc bends through the family twice: the indispensable financier, the enemies at court, the reckoning. In Vienna the debt was buried with the man; in Stuttgart the man was hung up as the debt.
